sections.title: The 'bár-... is' Architecture
sections.content: To express 'whoever', 'whatever', 'however', or 'no matter how much', Hungarian begins the subordinate clause with a 'bár-' indeterminate pronoun/adverb (bárki, bármi, bárhogyan, bármennyire, bármilyen + adj) and places the concessive particle 'is' right after the conjugated verb (or after the focused predicate before 'van'): 'Bármennyire igyekszik is...' (No matter how hard he tries...), 'Bármilyen képtelennek tűnik is...' (However absurd it may seem...).

sections.title: Indicative vs. Subjunctive in 'bár-' Clauses
sections.content: When the concession refers to an actual, ongoing, or past fact, Hungarian uses the indicative ('Bármit mondott is, nem hittem neki' — Whatever he said, I didn't believe him). When it projects a hypothetical extreme into the future or abstract space, it often uses the subjunctive/imperative ('Bárki jöjjön is, nyitva maradunk' — Whoever may come, we stay open).

sections.title: Universal Concessive Patterns
rows: Bárki kérdezi is, ugyanaz a válasz.
Whoever asks, the answer is the same.
Bármit írtak is a táblára, beállt a sorba.
Whatever they wrote on the sign, he got in line.
However much I respect the argument...
No matter how we twist and turn the words...

items.spanish: Bármennyire logikusnak látszik is a szabály, a gyakorlatban képtelenséghez vezet.
items.english: However logical the rule may seem, in practice it leads to absurdity.

items.spanish: Bárki vizsgálja is meg a levezetést, nem talál benne formai hibát.
items.english: Whoever examines the deduction finds no formal error in it.

items.spanish: Bárhogyan próbált is szabadulni a csapdából, mindig ugyanoda jutott vissza.
items.english: No matter how he tried to escape the trap, he always ended up back in the same place.

sections.title: B2 Stylistic Notice
sections.content: In careful literary Hungarian, place 'is' after the verb ('Bármit mondott is'), though in modern spoken Hungarian 'Bármit is mondott' is also frequently heard.
